about:
Hub is a private home base for a household: the people, plans, and paperwork that keep the place running. One household per instance, one login per person, and everything else — photos, calendars, mail, documents — pulled in from the self-hosted services you already run.

The dashboard is a shared chronicle: a journal with mentions, photos, comments, and reactions, alongside who lives here, what is coming up, and the photo days Hub thinks are worth writing up.
highlights: People and pets: contacts, places, health, education, and a derived family tree
Calendars of its own plus CalDAV, ICS subscriptions, and a wall-tablet kiosk view
Vaults for property, vehicles, insurance, accounts, and documents, with expiry reminders
Todos as kanban boards with checklists and links to any record
Pulls photos from Immich and documents from Paperless into the chronicle
Transcribes podcasts through Whisper

about:
Manor is a household's financial life in one place. It pulls bank, card, brokerage, crypto, property, and equity-compensation data into a single normalised ledger, keeps it current on its own, and gives you the views a good personal finance app would — cashflow, budget, subscriptions, net worth, portfolio performance, taxes.

Every number traces back to the transactions that produced it, and everything stays on your hardware. It is built for one household — a few people, one or more admins — so it favours clarity and correctness over multi-tenant scale.

Cashflow, budgets, subscriptions, and net worth over time

title: Immich
description: Photo & video library — phone backup, faces, and smart search.

spec.notes: Your first visit creates the admin account. Phone apps connect to this app's URL. The library lives in Drive under Apps → Immich, and snapshots include all of it — if it outgrows nightly backups, move the upload volume out of the app's own folder (its Drive tab → Move) and back that up separately. To let apps that use Immich (Once, Hub) in: create an API key in Immich (Account Settings → API Keys) and add it as the IMMICH_API_KEY secret in Config → Secrets; an app that declares uses: [immich] picks it up from fog. An app without that (or off fog) takes http://<this app's name>:2283 and the key in its own settings.

options.label: DB_PASSWORD
options.hint: Immich's private Postgres password.

about:
Immich is a photo and video library for a household — the self-hosted answer to Google Photos and iCloud. Phones back up to it automatically, and everything is searchable by person, place, date, or a plain description of what is in the picture.

It runs with its own database, cache, and a machine-learning service that recognises faces and objects on this machine, so nothing leaves the house to be indexed.
highlights: Automatic backup from the iOS and Android apps
Face recognition, smart search, and a map of where photos were taken
Shared albums, partner sharing, and public links
Timeline, memories, and duplicate detection
RAW, HEIC, live photos, and 360° images handled natively
Multi-user with per-user libraries and storage quotas

Automatic tagging and filing that learns from your corrections
A scans folder: drop a file in and it is consumed
Mail rules that fetch attachments from an inbox

title: OpenClaw
description: Personal AI assistant — chat with your agent over WhatsApp, Telegram, and the web, with memory and tools.

spec.notes: Installing runs OpenClaw's setup for you, so the gateway comes up configured. Give it the address of a model server on your own network — Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, or anything with an OpenAI-compatible API — and Fog finds it, picks a model that can use tools, and points the assistant at it; nothing leaves the house. An Anthropic key instead has it answer with Claude, and with neither it still boots so you can choose a provider in the Control UI. Name the assistant at install and it skips the first-run “who am I” interview; leave the name blank and it will ask you in your first conversation. First visit: the Control UI asks for the gateway token — copy it from Config → Secrets (OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN). From there, pair chat channels (WhatsApp, Telegram, …) in the dashboard. The Control UI needs a secure context, so reach it over HTTPS — set up a domain certificate in Fog if you haven't. Memory, sessions, and config live in the state volume and are included in backups.

options.label: Local LLM address
options.hint: IP, host, or URL of a model server on your network — Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (e.g. 192.0.2.10). Fog discovers its models and picks one. It has to listen on the network, not just localhost (Ollama needs OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0).

options.label: Anthropic API key
options.hint: Used when no local address is given. Leave both blank to choose a provider later in the Control UI.

options.label: Assistant's name
options.hint: What you'll call it. Left blank, it interviews you about who it should be in your first conversation.

options.label: Your name
options.hint: What the assistant calls you.

options.label: Local LLM model
options.hint: Model ID on that server, e.g. qwen3:8b. Blank picks the roomiest one that supports tool calling.

options.label: Local LLM API key
options.hint: Only for local gateways that ask for one (LiteLLM and friends) — Ollama and LM Studio don't.

options.label: Your pronouns
options.hint: So the assistant refers to you correctly.

options.label: Assistant's nature
options.hint: AI? robot? familiar? ghost in the machine?

options.label: Assistant's vibe
options.hint: How it comes across — sharp, warm, chaotic, calm.
options.default: warm, direct, and a little playful

options.label: Assistant's emoji
options.hint: Its signature.

options.label: OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN
options.hint: Protects the gateway's Control UI and API; unique per instance.

about:
OpenClaw is a personal AI assistant that lives on your own hardware and meets you where you already talk — WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, Slack, iMessage, and the web — with memory that persists between conversations and tools it can act with.

State, memory, and credentials stay on this machine. Models are plugins: point it at Claude, a local model, or whatever you prefer, and swap later without changing anything else.
highlights: One assistant across twenty-plus chat channels and native apps
Long-term memory and per-person context
Tools and skills: calendars, home automation, browsing, code
Any model provider, including ones running locally
No paid tier, hosted service, or token — stewarded by a foundation

about:
Hook is an acquisition engine for ebooks and audiobooks. You tell it what you want — a book, an author, a series — and it obtains the right edition from the usenet indexers you subscribe to, through the download client you already run, and hands the finished file to BookOrbit, where you actually read.

It fills the role Readarr played in a media stack, built so that a single closed metadata proxy can never kill it, and so that every step between “I want this” and “it is on my shelf” is legible and self-correcting.
highlights: Wants, profiles, and monitors for authors and series
A scored decision engine that explains every grab
A failure ladder that retries, substitutes, and asks for help in that order
Indexers from Prowlarr, downloads through SABnzbd, delivery to BookOrbit

title: HUD
description: Brings calendars, webhooks, and agents to the edge of attention — a BusyBar on the desk, a phone, the room's lights — without interrupting work.

HUD_MASTER_KEY encrypts every credential HUD stores — changing it makes them unreadable, so keep it with your backups. For Google Calendar, set GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET in Config → Secrets and redeploy; CalDAV and ICS feeds need neither. Apps run on bridge networking, so add the BusyBar by IP (give it a DHCP reservation) or use Scan on the Surfaces page. Add the deploy key and webhook (Overview tab) to the Gitea repo for push-to-deploy.

HUD brings timely information to the edge of attention without interrupting work. It connects sources — calendars, webhooks, agents — to surfaces — a BusyBar on the desk, a phone, the room's lights — through one pipeline of rules, so the next meeting counts down quietly instead of popping up over what you are doing.

Every notice can be traced back to the event and the rule that raised it, and rules are edited and simulated live in the console.

Lucid is how you see through the fog: one console for everything the apps on this server are doing — metrics, request traces, logs, continuous profiles, and visitor analytics, all behind one query bar.

about:
Fit is a household's health record on its own hardware. It pulls in Whoop, Withings and Apple Health, tracks medication and supplement regimens, and keeps every number traceable to the payload that produced it.

Health data stays in the house. Fit runs on a sealed network with no route out of the machine, answers on the home network only, and offers nothing to other apps. Morning briefs and lab reading use the household's own models or wait.

Apple Health and one-tap dose logging from the iPhone app

Offers its data to Fit alone

Model files are kept once for the house, on a NAS if you like, and copied to a Mac over the LAN instead of downloaded again. The same model compared across machines, with every setting that differs called out
Model files downloaded once for the house and copied over the LAN, checked by hash

One OpenAI-compatible endpoint for the house, routed to the Mac best placed to answer

title: SABnzbd
description: Usenet downloader.

files.name: host-whitelist-init
files.content:
#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bash
# Fog: SABnzbd refuses any request whose Host header it does not recognise —
# its DNS-rebind guard. Two names reach it: this app's own hostname behind
# Fog's proxy, and its name on the fog network ("sabnzbd"), which is how the
# apps that use it call its API. SABnzbd has no way to learn either, so fold
# both into host_whitelist before it starts; entries already there (the
# container's hostname, anything the operator added) are kept.
ini=/config/sabnzbd.ini
hosts=$(printf '%s,%s' "${FOG_FQDN:-}" "${FOG_NETWORK_NAME:-sabnzbd}" | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')

if [[ ! -f $ini ]]; then
    # First start: SABnzbd fills in every other default around this one.
    printf '[misc]\nhost_whitelist = %s\n' "$(printf '%s' "$hosts" | sed 's/^,//; s/,/, /g')" > "$ini"
    lsiown abc:abc "$ini"
    exit 0
fi

tmp=$(mktemp)
awk -v hosts="$hosts" '
{
    line[NR] = $0
    if ($0 ~ /^host_whitelist[ \t]*=/) wl = NR
    else if ($0 ~ /^\[misc\][ \t]*$/) misc = NR
}
END {
    if (wl) { cur = line[wl]; sub(/^host_whitelist[ \t]*=[ \t]*/, "", cur) }
    n = split(cur "," hosts, part, ",")
    for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        gsub(/^[ \t]+|[ \t]+$/, "", part[i])
        if (part[i] != "" && !seen[part[i]]++) list = list (list == "" ? "" : ", ") part[i]
    }
    entry = "host_whitelist = " list
    last = NR
    if (wl) line[wl] = entry
    else if (misc) line[misc] = line[misc] "\n" entry
    else { last = NR + 1; line[last] = "[misc]\n" entry }
    for (i = 1; i <= last; i++) print line[i]
}' "$ini" > "$tmp"

# Rewrite only on a real change, and in place, so the file keeps the
# ownership SABnzbd needs to save its own config over it later.
if [[ -s $tmp ]] && ! cmp -s "$tmp" "$ini"; then
    cat "$tmp" > "$ini"
fi
rm -f "$tmp"

files.name: api-key-init
files.content:
#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bash
# Fog: SABnzbd's API key is SABNZBD_API_KEY from Fog's vault, the one Fog
# hands to apps it connects to SABnzbd. Unset, SABnzbd keeps its own.
ini=/config/sabnzbd.ini
key=${SABNZBD_API_KEY:-}
[[ -n $key ]] || exit 0

if [[ ! -f $ini ]]; then
    printf '[misc]\napi_key = %s\n' "$key" > "$ini"
    lsiown abc:abc "$ini"
    exit 0
fi

tmp=$(mktemp)
awk -v key="$key" '
{
    line[NR] = $0
    if ($0 ~ /^api_key[ \t]*=/ && !ak) ak = NR
    else if ($0 ~ /^\[misc\][ \t]*$/) misc = NR
}
END {
    entry = "api_key = " key
    last = NR
    if (ak) line[ak] = entry
    else if (misc) line[misc] = line[misc] "\n" entry
    else { last = NR + 1; line[last] = "[misc]\n" entry }
    for (i = 1; i <= last; i++) print line[i]
}' "$ini" > "$tmp"

if [[ -s $tmp ]] && ! cmp -s "$tmp" "$ini"; then
    cat "$tmp" > "$ini"
fi
rm -f "$tmp"

files.name: folders-init
files.content:
#!/usr/bin/with-contenv bash
# Fog: downloads must land in /data, the folder Fog shares with the apps
# that use SABnzbd (Hook reads finished files there). Point download_dir
# and complete_dir into it unless they already are.
ini=/config/sabnzbd.ini
shared=/data
if [[ ! -f $ini ]]; then
    printf '[misc]\n' > "$ini"
    lsiown abc:abc "$ini"
fi

tmp=$(mktemp)
awk -v shared="$shared" '
function inside(v) { return v == shared || index(v, shared "/") == 1 }
function value(l) { sub(/^[^=]*=[ \t]*/, "", l); return l }
{
    line[NR] = $0
    if ($0 ~ /^download_dir[ \t]*=/) dd = NR
    else if ($0 ~ /^complete_dir[ \t]*=/) cd = NR
    else if ($0 ~ /^\[misc\][ \t]*$/ && !misc) misc = NR
}
END {
    last = NR
    if (!misc) { last = NR + 1; line[last] = "[misc]"; misc = last }
    add = ""
    if (!dd) add = add "\ndownload_dir = " shared "/incomplete"
    else if (!inside(value(line[dd]))) line[dd] = "download_dir = " shared "/incomplete"
    if (!cd) add = add "\ncomplete_dir = " shared "/complete"
    else if (!inside(value(line[cd]))) line[cd] = "complete_dir = " shared "/complete"
    line[misc] = line[misc] add
    for (i = 1; i <= last; i++) print line[i]
}' "$ini" > "$tmp"

if [[ -s $tmp ]] && ! cmp -s "$tmp" "$ini"; then
    cat "$tmp" > "$ini"
fi
rm -f "$tmp"

for key in download_dir complete_dir; do
    dir=$(sed -n "s/^$key[[:space:]]*=[[:space:]]*//p" "$ini" | head -n1)
    if [[ $dir == "$shared" || $dir == "$shared"/* ]]; then
        mkdir -p "$dir" && lsiown abc:abc "$dir"
    fi
done
exit 0

Categories with per-category folders and scripts
Bandwidth scheduling and pause on demand
A responsive interface with a night mode
Fog whitelists its own hostname on install

Jellyfin is a media server: your films, series, and music, streamed to any screen in the house and beyond. Point it at the media folder and it fetches artwork and metadata, tracks what everyone has watched, and plays to the TV, the phone, and the browser.

It is the free and open alternative to Plex and Emby — no account with anyone, no features held back, no phoning home.
highlights: Apps for every TV platform, phone, and browser
Artwork, metadata, and subtitles fetched automatically
Per-user libraries, parental controls, and watch history
Hardware transcoding where the machine allows it
Live TV and DVR with a tuner
SyncPlay to watch together from different rooms

Navidrome streams your music collection. It scans the music folder, keeps up with additions, and plays through its own web player or any of the many apps that speak the Subsonic API — on the phone, in the car, on the desktop.

It is light enough to run on anything and fast with libraries of a hundred thousand tracks.
highlights: Works with dozens of Subsonic-compatible apps
Scans the folder in the background and picks up changes
Playlists, smart playlists, favourites, and ratings per user
Transcoding on the fly for slow links
Last.fm and ListenBrainz scrobbling

The web player on a phone

title: Audiobookshelf
description: Audiobook and podcast server.

options.label: Audiobook folder

about:
Audiobookshelf is a server for audiobooks and podcasts. It organises the library, keeps everyone's listening position, and plays through its own apps on iPhone and Android or in the browser — with downloads for offline listening.

Podcasts are fetched and kept on schedule, and metadata and covers come from the usual sources.
highlights: Progress synced across the web and the phone apps
Podcast subscriptions with automatic downloads
Chapters, bookmarks, and playback speed
Metadata and covers from Audible, iTunes, and more
Multi-user with per-user progress and libraries
Ebook reading too

Your books live in Drive → Content → Books, which BookOrbit sees as /books — create a library pointing there and drop ebooks into the folder from the Drive page. about:
BookOrbit is a library and reading platform for ebooks, PDFs, audiobooks, and comics. It organises what you own and lets you read it anywhere — the web, an iPhone, an Apple Watch, a Kobo, or KOReader — with progress, highlights, and status kept in sync between them.

Around that core sit metadata from a dozen providers, reading statistics, OPDS and send-to-Kindle delivery, and multi-user accounts, all on your own hardware.

Three-way sync between Kobo, KOReader, and the web reader
Native iPhone and Apple Watch apps with offline downloads
Metadata from fourteen providers, reading stats, and achievements
OPDS, send-to-Kindle, and sync out to Hardcover, Readwise, and StoryGraph
Where Hook delivers the books it finds

screenshots.alt: The dashboard: reading stats, widgets, and shelves
BookOrbit on iPhone and Apple Watch
The KOReader plugin on an e-reader

title: Uptime Kuma
description: Uptime monitoring with status pages and alerts.
about:
Uptime Kuma watches the things you care about and tells you when they go down. Give it a URL, a host, a port, or a container, and it checks on an interval, keeps the history, and notifies you the moment something changes.

It also publishes status pages — a tidy public view of what is up for the household or for people you host things for.
highlights: HTTP, TCP, ping, DNS, Docker, and keyword monitors
Ninety notification services, ntfy among them
Status pages with incidents and maintenance windows
Response-time charts and certificate expiry warnings

title: Vaultwarden
description: Bitwarden-compatible password manager server.
about:
Vaultwarden is a password manager server that speaks Bitwarden's protocol. The official Bitwarden apps and browser extensions connect to it as if it were bitwarden.com — but the vault is here, encrypted with keys that never leave your devices.

It is written in Rust, needs a fraction of the resources of the upstream server, and includes the features Bitwarden charges for.
highlights: Works with every official Bitwarden app and extension
Organisations and collections for sharing within the household
Two-factor sign-in, emergency access, and Send
Admin page for users and settings

title: ntfy
description: Push notifications you can point Fog and your other apps at.
about:
ntfy is push notifications with nothing in the way. Publish a message to a topic with a single HTTP request — from a script, a cron job, or any of the apps here — and it arrives on your phone and desktop.

Feed, Hook, Uptime Kuma, and Jellyseerr can all be pointed at it, and Fog can send its own alerts here too.
highlights: Publish with curl; receive in the iOS and Android apps or the browser
Topics with access control
Priorities, tags, attachments, and action buttons
Scheduled delivery and email forwarding

title: AdGuard Home
description: Network-wide ad and tracker blocking — a DNS server for your whole LAN.

spec.notes: In the setup wizard, set the Admin Web Interface port to **3000** (it defaults to 80) — that's the port Fog's route points at; the DNS listen interface and port 53 are fine as offered. Then point clients at this server: either set your router's DHCP DNS to this server's IP, or change DNS per device. If port 53 is already taken on the host (e.g. systemd-resolved's stub listener or another DNS server), free it first or the app won't start.

about:
AdGuard Home blocks ads and trackers for every device on the network at once. It runs as your DNS server: point the router at it and phones, TVs, and laptops stop resolving ad domains without any software installed on them.

It also gives you a view of what the devices in the house are talking to, and lets you block or allow per client.
highlights: Network-wide blocking with no client software
Per-client rules and parental controls
Encrypted upstream DNS (DoH, DoT, DoQ)
Query log and statistics
Publishes port 53 on this machine

title: Home Assistant
description: Home automation hub. (Bridge networking — some discovery integrations may need extra setup.)

spec.notes: To let apps such as HUD use Home Assistant, create a long-lived access token (your profile → Security) and add it as the HASS_TOKEN secret in Config → Secrets.

about:
Home Assistant is the home-automation hub: lights, thermostats, locks, cameras, sensors, and media, from thousands of brands, brought under one roof and one interface, with automations that run locally.

Fog runs it on the container network, so integrations that discover devices by broadcast may need to be added by address instead.
highlights: Thousands of integrations, most working locally
Automations, scenes, and scripts with a visual editor
Dashboards for phones, tablets, and wall panels
Energy monitoring
Voice assistants that stay in the house

title: Homepage
description: A tidy dashboard for everything running on this server.
about:
Homepage is a start page for everything running on this server: one tidy grid of the apps, with live status and a few numbers from each — downloads in progress, films requested, uptime — so a household can find its way around without bookmarks.

It is configured in YAML, and it reads directly from the apps it lists through their APIs.
highlights: Widgets for a hundred-plus services, including everything in this store
Docker integration: shows what is running
Bookmarks, search, and weather
Themes and backgrounds

title: Gotenberg
description: Document conversion API: HTML and Office files to PDF via Chromium and LibreOffice.
about:
Gotenberg is a document conversion service: an HTTP API in front of Chromium and LibreOffice that turns HTML, Markdown, Office files, and URLs into PDF, and converts between document formats.

It has no interface of its own. Office uses it for exact PDF export and for opening .doc, .odt, and .rtf; anything else on this machine can use it too.
highlights: HTML, Markdown, and URLs to PDF through Chromium
Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and OpenDocument to PDF through LibreOffice
Merge, split, and PDF/A conversion
Stateless: nothing to store, nothing to back up

title: n8n
description: Workflow automation — connect apps and services with visual flows, webhooks, schedules, and AI agents.

spec.notes: First visit: n8n asks you to create the owner account — do it right away, since whoever gets there first owns the instance. Webhook URLs use this app's HTTPS address, so services outside the house can reach them only if Fog serves this app publicly. Reach the editor over HTTPS at the hostname Fog serves it on: n8n's session cookie is secure-only, so plain http:// will not keep you signed in. Workflows, credentials, and execution history live in Fog's Postgres and are in the app's backups; N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY in Config → Secrets encrypts the stored credentials, so never change it after setup.

options.label: Timezone
options.hint: Schedule triggers fire in this zone.

options.label: N8N_ENCRYPTION_KEY
options.hint: Encrypts stored credentials; never change it after setup.

about:
n8n is a workflow automation tool: you draw a flow of nodes on a canvas — a trigger, then steps that fetch, transform, decide, and send — and it runs whenever the trigger fires. A webhook, a schedule, a new email, or a message in a chat can start one, and its 400-odd integrations reach most services a household uses.

When a node doesn't exist for what you need, a Code node takes JavaScript or Python, and an HTTP Request node talks to any API. AI agent nodes put a language model in the middle of a flow, with your other nodes as its tools.
highlights: A visual editor for flows, with every run's data inspectable step by step
Triggers from webhooks, schedules, email, and hundreds of services
Code nodes in JavaScript or Python when a built-in node isn't enough
AI agents that call your workflows and integrations as tools
Credentials encrypted at rest in Fog's Postgres

screenshots.alt: A workflow that drafts email replies with an AI model

title: Gitea
description: Git hosting with pull requests, issues, and a package registry.

spec.notes: The first account to register becomes the administrator, so register yours right away, then close registration if this server is reachable beyond the household (Site Administration → Configuration, or set `GITEA__service__DISABLE_REGISTRATION` to `true` in the app's env). Clone over HTTPS at this app's URL, or over SSH on port **2222** — add your public key under Settings → SSH / GPG Keys. Repositories, the database, and the config all live in the data volume, so snapshots capture the whole instance.

about:
Gitea is a git host with the trimmings: repositories, pull requests, issues, a package registry, and Actions, in a single light binary. It is where the household's own code lives — and the household's own apps — Hub, Manor, Office, Feed, Hook — deploy from a Gitea just like it.

Fog configures it from the environment on every boot, so the clone URLs it prints follow the address you give it.
highlights: Pull requests, code review, and protected branches
Issues, milestones, labels, and a wiki per repository
Actions compatible with GitHub workflows
Package registry for containers, npm, and more
Clone over HTTPS at this app's address, or SSH on port 2222

title: VS Code
description: VS Code in the browser — edit code, run a terminal, and install extensions from any machine.

spec.notes: Sign in with the password in Config → Secrets (PASSWORD). The terminal is a shell inside this app's container, so anyone with the password can run commands there — keep it strong, and don't share it beyond the people you'd give a login on this server. Extensions come from Open VSX, the open marketplace, rather than Microsoft's, so a few Microsoft-only ones (Copilot, Pylance, Remote-SSH) aren't available. Previews and extension pages need a secure context, so reach it over HTTPS at the hostname Fog serves it on. Your projects live in /config/workspace, and settings, extensions, and workspace are all included in backups. To use sudo in the terminal, set SUDO_PASSWORD in Config → Secrets and redeploy.

options.hint: The editor's sign-in password; copy it from Config → Secrets after install.

about:
VS Code, the editor, running on this server and used from a browser tab. Open it from a laptop, a tablet, or a borrowed machine and your files, settings, extensions, and terminal are exactly where you left them — the work happens here, not on whatever you're typing on.

It is code-server, the open-source build of VS Code that Coder packages for the web. Extensions install from Open VSX, so most of the usual ones are there; a few Microsoft-only ones are not.
highlights: The full VS Code editor, with its settings, themes, and keybindings
An integrated terminal on the server itself
Extensions from the Open VSX marketplace
Git built in: stage, commit, and push from the sidebar
Everything under one volume, so backups carry your whole setup
